S012.name: Feeling_Restless
S012.description: Often runs about or climbs in situations where it is inappropriate. (Note: In adolescents or adults, may be limited to feeling restless.)
examples: Feels uncomfortable and restless as if something is squirming inside when sitting still.
Feels internally anxious and stifled in situations requiring prolonged sitting.
A sense of urgency and anxiety that one must keep moving or doing something.
Feels unable to endure staying still and must constantly be doing something.

S013.name: Quiet_Activity_Difficulty
S013.description: Often unable to play or engage in leisure activities quietly.
examples: Unable to engage in calm activities for long, such as reading quietly or drawing.
Cannot play quietly, often shouting or making loud noises during games or play.
Unable to stay quiet in quiet places like libraries or movie theaters, making noise.
Cannot endure and avoids quiet and calm activities like meditation or yoga.

S014.name: Constant_Activity
S014.description: Is often 'on the go', acting as if 'driven by a motor'.
examples: Constantly moving and active as if driven by a motor.
Starts another task immediately after finishing one, without resting for a moment.
Unable to stay still even on weekends or days off, constantly doing something.
Appears to others to be always busy and bustling about.

S016.name: Blurting_Answers
S016.description: Often blurts out an answer before a question has been completed.
examples: Raises hand or blurts out the answer before the question is even finished in class or meetings.
Jumps to conclusions and speaks before the other person finishes their sentence.
Answers hastily without reading the question to the end in quizzes or exams.
Interrupts and answers in the middle of a conversation without listening to the other person until the end.

S017.name: Waiting_Turn_Difficulty
S017.description: Often has difficulty waiting his or her turn.
examples: Cannot wait and cuts in line or gets impatient when standing in a queue.
Rushes or cuts in without waiting for their turn in games or board games.
Keeps checking the time or complaining when waiting for their turn at hospitals or public offices.
Fidgets, complains, or gets annoyed in situations where waiting for a turn is required.

symptom.disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Hyperactive/Impulsive Presentation) is characterized by a persistent pattern of excessive motor activity, restlessness, impulsive actions, and difficulty inhibiting behavior, with relatively fewer or less prominent inattentive symptoms. It typically has onset in childhood, but may only become clinically recognized later when environmental demands for sustained self-control increase, such as in structured work or academic settings. The course is often chronic, with some individuals showing partial remission or a shift in symptom expression (e.g., from overt running/climbing to an internal sense of restlessness) across the lifespan. It is distinguished from mood, anxiety, or personality disorders by its early onset, pervasive pattern across settings, and the specific clustering of hyperactive and impulsive behaviors rather than episodic or situational overactivity.

patient.stressor: Jorge entered his radiologic technology program 17 months ago, transitioning from a more flexible high school routine into tightly scheduled labs, lectures, and clinical rotations that required careful adherence to protocols and respectful pacing during patient interactions. While his artistic and technical skills with imaging flourished, instructors repeatedly noted that he rushed through instructions, jumped into procedures before being fully briefed, and had difficulty staying in his seat during long lectures and safety trainings, which raised concerns about patient safety and professional conduct. Over the next year, these issues escalated: he received written warnings for interrupting supervisors, cutting off patients mid-explanation, and struggling to wait during team huddles, ultimately being told that his spot in the program might be at risk if he couldn’t regulate his behavior. Feeling distressed that his dream career in radiology was jeopardized and after a clinical preceptor suggested that his lifelong tendency to be "on the go" might reflect more than just nerves, he agreed to see a psychiatrist through the college health service.
patient.chief_complaint: “In class and in the hospital, I keep jumping in and answering or talking before people even finish their questions, and it’s getting me into trouble.”
